why: A homestead grove is one farm's own wood; a shelter belt is shared by a settlement on one or two windward sides.
A homestead grove is one farm's wood; the woodland commons is the village's shared wood for fuel and litter, away from the houses.
A homestead grove is one farm's wood; a shared bamboo grove is a stand of bamboo held in common.
The lot is the whole plot the farm stood on (100-300 tsubo); the yard is the threshing floor in it (20-30 tsubo).
The first is how much of one walled compound its buildings cover; the second is how densely a whole city quarter is built.
A magistrate's compound is a county or intendant's office; a governor's is the provincial seat, drawn larger.
The nagaya-mon is a compound's front gate through a range of gatekeepers' rooms; a nagaya is a long lodging building of its own, not a gate.
The gate's bansho is a compound's gatekeepers' guardroom; a border post is a checkpoint on a road at a domain's boundary.
The genkan is the stepped entrance of the house itself; the main gate is the opening in the compound's wall, across open ground from it.
The office hall is the whole working building and its staff; the hearing court is where hearings were held, against the front of that hall.
Holding cells are a magistracy's small remand cell in its own compound; the city jail is a walled court of the governor's compound or a compound of its own.
The first is the chain of storehouses the tax rice passed through; the second is the village's own shared store and where it stood.
The first is the lord's and magistrate's storehouses for tax rice on its way out; the second is a capital's wharf granary, with the Emperor's separate granaries.
The first is the earth-walled storehouse as the answer to fire; the second is the chain of storehouses the tax rice passed through.
The first is the shrine inside a magistrate's office compound; the second is a farmstead's own household shrine.
The first is the samurai house itself and its rooms; the second is a city samurai's lot, and the house's share of it, by rank.
The butsuma is a Buddhist room inside the house holding the tablets of its dead; a yashikigami is a Shinto god's small shrine in the grounds.
The kitchen door is the kitchen's own service door; the genkan is the formal entrance for guests of rank.
The first is a samurai residence's own bath room; the sento is a town's commercial bathhouse open to anyone who pays.
The first is a samurai residence's bath; the second is a farm's bath, a room at the farmhouse or a shed in its yard.
The first is a samurai residence's privies; the second is a farm's privy and its night-soil store.
The first is a samurai residence's privies; the second is a town house's and a tenement's shared privy, and the carters in town.
The first is the ornamental garden looked at from the formal rooms; the second is the household's worked vegetable plot.
The first covers the stone lantern in a residence's garden; the second the votive lanterns villagers gave to line a shrine's approach.
The first is a plot inside a walled samurai or office compound; the second is a farmhouse's kitchen plot by its door.
The first is where the one chief retainer lived; the second is how a compound's staff in general were housed.
A warrior's or official's own stable inside a compound, against a post town's stable for the relay horses of travelers.
The rowhouse an official's staff lived in inside a government compound, against a samurai household's domestic servants inside their master's walls.
The staff rowhouse inside an office's compound, against the foot soldiers' ranked small houses at a castle town's edge.
The first is where samurai trained in halls and dojos; the second is a city's open drill, riding and archery grounds as a quarter of ground.
A domain's guard post where its road crosses into another territory, against a town's own gate or entry post; bansho names both.
The first is where two sides met to deal across a border; the second is the border line itself and its markers.
The post that examined those crossing, against the place where two sides met to negotiate.
The first is one samurai family's manor among its fields; the second is where a city's gentry and samurai estates stand around it.
An ordinary merchant's shop-front townhouse on the street vs a rich merchant's walled compound with storehouses.
A commercial inn for any paying traveler vs the official lodging kept for lords and officials.
The first is an inn's building and its plan; the second is how many inns and cheap lodging houses a place kept, and where.
A communal well is the households' draw-point among the houses; a field well lifts irrigation water onto a crop in the field.
A communal well is shared by commoner households; a samurai household's well is its own, inside its fence.
The first is the watch for fire - tower, alarm bell and gear; the second is the night watch against crime - ward gates, keepers' huts and watchmen.
The first is how a town watched for and fought fire in its streets; the second is how one owner kept goods from fire in a plastered storehouse.
The first is the civic tower that struck the hours; the second is the lookout that watched for fire and rang the alarm bell.
The terakoya is the commoners' one-room writing school; the hanko is a domain's school for its retainers' sons, with buildings of its own.
The first is which trades a place keeps and the shop as its keeper's house; the second is how a street's frontage is divided among rich and poor.
The first is the smith's own premises and the farrier's shed; the second counts the smith among a place's trades.
A brewery brewed sake in its own vat hall under license; the village sake shop only sold it.
The first is a town's and city's public eating and drinking houses; the second includes the teahouses a highway village sets at its street ends in place of an inn.
The first is the dyer's own premises, vats and drying ground; the second counts the dyer among a place's trades.
The yard is the open working ground beside a stable where animals are tied and watered; the stable is the building with its stalls.
The charcoal yard is a town's depot where baled charcoal is stored and sold; the kiln is where charcoal is burned, in the hill wood.
A refining forge turns pig iron into wrought-iron bar on two hearths; a smith forges tools and shoes from bar iron at a single forge.
The tanning yard is the riverside works where hides were soaked; the outcaste quarter is where the tanners lived.
The first is the outcaste quarter's site and buildings; the second is the legally zoned samurai ground of a city.
The grounds are where a sentence is carried out or displayed; the jail holds the accused and condemned until then.
A roofed playhouse is a great city's permanent licensed theater; a town's stage is an open stage on shrine ground or a temporary hut.
The agreed line between two domains and its markers, against the guarded post where a road crosses that line.
The first is a county seat's or post town's census with its farmers; the second gives the walled provincial city's inhabitants, with no farmer households.
The first is the town's overall plan; the second is its street net, the count of cross streets and the cranked ends of its road.
The first is a town's strip along its road and its packed street front; the second is a walled city quarter's built share and open ground.
The first is a county seat's wall or a town's earth bank; the second is a provincial city's ring wall and its gates.
The first is where the compound stands in its town and which way it faces; the second is what stood inside its walls.
The first sorts a town's ground into bands back from the street; the second gives each wealth band's frontage width.
The same sorting of shops and poor housing, in a town and in a city.
The first is the row of houses along a town's street; the second is one merchant's house from shop front to back of lot.
The first is a town's street front, wall to wall only on a busy road; the second is the city's continuous street walls.
The townsmen's rented back-lot tenements, against the rows a samurai residence or office builds for its own staff.
A merchant's small court and back garden in a town, against a farmhouse's vegetable garden by its door.
A commoner's court of one or two tsubo inside the house, against the ornamental garden of a samurai residence or government post.
A town's privies and the dealers who carried the night soil off, against a farm's privy whose night soil stayed on the farm.
The first is the office a ward's commoners kept; the second is the ward itself, its officers and how many a city has.
The first is the commoners' own office; the second is the lord's or the state's seat of government.
The periodic market villagers come in for on market day, vs the standing shops outside a walled town's gate that serve the road every day.
A county town's few shops strung along the road outside its gate, vs a city's larger gate suburb with its kilns and swallowed villages.
The inns and cheap lodgings any paying traveler used vs the official lodging kept for lords and officials.
The inns and lodging houses themselves, wherever they stood, vs the strip of shops and inns along the road outside a walled town's gate.
The honjin lodged travelers of rank; the relay station kept and dispatched the horses and men that carried travelers on.
The relay station, its office and stable building, vs the open working ground beside a stable where animals are tied and watered.
Market vegetable plots in the fields at a town's edge, against a townsman's small garden behind the shop.
A town's worked fuel wood and cut grass beyond its fields, against the grove planted around each farmhouse.
The farming households around a town's paddies, against the suburb of shops and inns outside its gate.
The first is a road town's fodder meadow for its horses and its hay stores; the second is the common coppice and cut grass on a town's margin.
The first is a road town's fodder ground for its post horses; the second is a farming village's common grass ground for fodder and green manure.
The first is what stood inside a shrine's ground; the second is where the shrine stood and how large its ground was.
The first is a village's own shrine and its furnishings; the second is the shrine inside a magistrate's or an office's walls.
A shrine wood is sacred ground around a shrine, following the slope; a homestead grove is a farmhouse windbreak, following the wind.
The first is who kept the shrine and the dwelling they lived in (kuri); the second is the halls and precinct the villagers used.
A street jizo or Inari is a wayside shrine; a town's own shrine is its district shrine or a small shrine on its own plot.
The first is the roadside stones and halls themselves; the second is where a village's boundary lies on each road that the boundary god marks.
The first includes the City God temple as a Chinese seat's principal shrine; the second is the state cult's altars and official temples.
A village temple is a Buddhist parish temple; a village shrine is the house of the local kami, which in the setting does the temple's work.
A town monastery is an Order's preceptor's house in a county town; a village temple is a village's own parish temple, which the setting replaces with the shrine.
A temple quarter is a district where a lord gathered many temples; a gate-front town is the houses and shops along one temple's approach.
A temple's bell tower hangs its bell inside its precinct; the bell-and-drum tower is the civic tower of a walled seat, apart from any temple.
The first is what one temple precinct holds and how big it is; the second is how many temples a city had and where they clustered.
The first is a city temple's clergy, celibate and married; the second is the one celibate country monk who keeps a village shrine or temple.
The first is the Confucian temple where Confucius was worshipped by the state; the second is the school where students were taught.
The first is the Chinese state's temples and altars, which the setting lacks; the second is the Buddhist monastery our maps draw in their place.
The burial ground is where the dead or their urns lie; the cremation ground is where the body is burned first, a separate feature.
The first is the burial ground itself - size, distance, shape; the second is which form of ground a village's dead lie in.
The burial ground is where remains are interred; the cremation ground is where the body is burned; the one word sanmai named either.
A bone mound is one low mound over the gathered bones of the unclaimed dead; a pauper burial ground is a fenced field of separate graves.
A town's or city's burial grounds and charity grounds, against a village's own communal ground.
The first is every way a capital's program departs from a provincial city's; the second is only the mix of its samurai housing.
The castle's own moat rings its baileys inside the city; the city's moat rings the city's outer wall.
The first is what stood within the castle's walls; the second is the castle as a whole - its seat, area, walls, moats and gates.
The first is the setting's Imperial office, one per domain at its capital; the second is a city's own police magistracy under its lord.
The first is how a domain capital's senior-heavy samurai are housed; the second is a samurai's lot and house by rank in any castle town.
The first is the castle town's domain time bell; the second is the combined bell-and-drum tower every walled seat keeps.
The first is the whole school of letters with its martial halls; the second is the martial halls and dojos where samurai trained.
A towpath is a narrow bank path for hauling boats upstream; a highway is a trunk road for overland travel.
The city's own wall round the whole city, against the castle's walls round the lord's seat inside it.
A gate tower stands over a gate's passage; a mamian is a tower projecting from the wall's face between the gates.
A post town's mitsuke is a pair of open banks marking where the town begins; a barrier or guard post is a gate that is shut and kept.
The walled court before a gate, with its own second gate, vs the gate's own passage, tower and moat crossing.
A defensive court before a gate vs the posts that watched who came through; mitsuke named both a masugata gate and a post town's banks.
A block is the ground a grid of streets encloses; a ward (machi) was the two sides of one street, facing across it.
The first is who stands where on a block; the second is how the street front is built.
The first is a city's wards and their night gates; the second is a town's night barring and the watchmen who kept it.
The first is the Imperial road's stretch inside a city, lined with shops; the second is the trunk road across the country.
The first is the one through-road and its market street; the second is the row of shophouses fronting every city street.
The first is the earthen storehouses behind a merchant's lot; the second is fire discipline in an administrative compound.
The first is a governor's compound in a provincial city; the second is the county magistrate's smaller manor in a county town.
The six ministries' own offices, against the governor's compound they stand around.
The ministries stand outside the castle on a capital map; the council of senior retainers met inside it.
The jail holds prisoners for the Ministry of Justice; a watch house or guard box is a street post of the watch, with no cells.
The first is a provincial city's samurai district; the second is a domain capital's, with its lineage compounds and walled estates.
The first is who lives in the samurai district and where; the second is the townsmen's ward and its gates.
The first is one samurai's lot and house by rank; the second is the district all the city's samurai houses make up.
The first is the soldiers a city kept under arms; the second is the hired servants who lived inside a samurai's own plot.
A city's tile kilns at its edge vs a potter's climbing-kiln works with its potters living at it.
The first is ground farmed inside a city's wall by its own households; the second is the farmland outside it, worked by villagers.
The first is the gardens inside a city's wall; the second is the vegetable belt outside a town's last houses.
The first is a landholding family's seat in the countryside by its fields; the second is a lord's suburban second house with gardens.
Where the canal opens on the river, against where it passes through the city's wall (the water gate).
The small loading basins cut off a canal's side, against the larger boat-entry dock and quays a city keeps.
A water gate is the passage through the wall for a canal and its boats; a city gate is the road's opening, tower and moat crossing.
The first is the gates on a moat's water and how they were worked; the second is where a moat's water comes from.
The landing is where boats load and unload; the towpath is the route along the bank from which boats were hauled upstream.
The landing is the bank where any cargo comes ashore; the rice storehouses are the capital's granary the rice wharf fills.
The watch post is a hut where boats were inspected; a water gate is the gate in a wall or channel that lets boats or water through.
The boatmen's shrine is the boatmen's water god kept by the landing; a town shrine is the quarter's or the city's own.
The landing market is a city's standing wholesale market; a town's market is periodic, held on set days in its street.
How many of a city's inhabitants live outside its wall, against what stands on the ground outside its gates.
The whole population a wall is sized to hold, against the samurai's share of it and where they live.
The share of a walled city's ground left unbuilt and how densely the rest is built, against the farmland and gardens on the unbuilt ground.
The first is the open ground kept around a shrine's buildings and graves; the second is the preserved grove the precinct stands in.
The first is whether the ground round a shrine or grave was kept swept; the second is what stood within the precinct.
The first is the farm household and its roofs; the second is the dependents and tenants who lived in huts on another's plot.
Every paddy stands flooded while its rice grows; a wet paddy stays waterlogged even when no rice is growing.
A paddy bund is the shared wall between two paddy basins; the channel-bank bund edges a ditch or canal.
The walking bund carries the way among the paddies; a village lane runs among the houses and across the dry fields.
The dry paddy drains to a field and can carry a winter crop; the wet paddy stays waterlogged all year and cannot.
The straw rick is threshed straw stacked on the reaped paddy; the drying rack holds unthreshed sheaves while they dry.
A wet paddy is cropped rice land on ground that never drains; a marsh is wetland not made into paddy.
An in-field pond is a small pocket of water inside one low paddy plot; a reservoir is the village's water store at the head of the system.
A dry field is never flooded; a paddy drained after the rice and worked for a winter crop is still paddy.
A dry field is a grain or bean plot away from the house; the kitchen bed is the household's small plot of greens at its house.
A tract is the whole field system one work waters; a plot is one leveled cell within it.
Temple fields are tax-free farmland out among the village's fields; a shrine's grounds are its precinct around the halls.
The canals bring water in along the high ground; the drain takes spent water out along the lowest line.
The fork of a settlement's head race into its canals is layout; dividing a ditch's water between villages by rule and rotation is sharing.
The first is the works where water is taken off the brook; the second is the dug network below it that delivers the water.
A village's reed marsh was cut every winter; the reed fringing a reservoir pond's shore is not recorded as cut.
The widths of every channel from field ditch to castle moat, vs a city's boat canals, their banks and frontage.
The first is the angle at which any channel leaves or joins another; the second is the intake and weir at a ditch's head.
The first covers how a moat's river ends meet the river; the second is whether water moves through a moat and where it comes from.
The mizuguchi is a paddy's own small inlet in its bund; the toshuko is the village's intake where the head race leaves the brook.
The first lifts water from a ditch onto a paddy by foot, hand or ox; the second uses a stream's fall to turn a wheel that pounds or grinds grain.
A washing place is a footing on running water for washing vegetables and clothes; a communal well is the shared source of drinking water.
A waju's ring dike encloses villages and fields already on the plain; a polder's dike encloses land reclaimed from marsh or lake.
The marsh is wet ground left below the fields; a reservoir pond is open water held behind a dike above the fields.
The first is what was kept off wet ground and where it stood instead; the second is the wet ground itself.
A moat is the defensive ditch ringing a wall or castle; a reservoir pond is water held behind a dike for irrigation alone.
Tea planted as a row on the banks between paddies vs tea planted on the dike round a fish pond.
Mulberry as a cash crop on a polder's dike crest vs the trees planted to hold the dike.
The first is rice land without a broad valley floor - hillside benches or narrow valley paddies; the second is the paddy in general.
The first is the diked farmland and its water; the second is how a river-plain village defended itself against flood.
The first is the whole diked block, a great dike round many fields; the second is the fish ponds dug inside it, each ringed by a small dike.
The first is how a polder's land was cut into parcels and held; the second is the bund itself in any paddy.
The dike's trees are low, cut and bare in winter, planted to hold the bank; the shelter belt is a tall grove planted to break the wind.
The polder's ring dike encloses many fields; a dike-pond's bank rings a single fish pond, heaped from its own mud.
The silk village's half-buried night-soil jar against the rice farm's muck heap in the yard.
The crop field on the bank round each fish pond vs the willow and mulberry rows planted along a polder's outer dike to hold it.
What grew on a pond's dike vs the pond-and-dike system itself, its sizes and sluices.
The first is the young fish and the small ponds they were reared in; the second is the grow-out pond with its planted dike.
The first is the sty on a fish-pond bank; the second is the pigs and ducks of a plain rice village with no fish ponds.
The first is how every caption is placed by its feature; the second is which buildings a caption may cover on a crowded sheet, and district names.
The first is a farming household's plot; the second is a samurai's house and rooms - yashiki names both.
The first is the plot and the buildings on it; the second is the family that lived there and its second roof.
The dwelling itself against the whole plot and everything on it, the farmhouse being one building of several.
The first is a well-off farm's fireproof earth-walled storehouse; the second is the plain wooden shed or barn for crop and tools.
The first is one well-off farm household's own storehouse; the second is the village's shared granary.
The first is a farm household's own storehouse; the second is the chain of storehouses the tax rice passed through.
Umaya names both: a farm's stall for its ox or horse, against a warrior's or office's stable for riding horses.
The privy and its night-soil tank or pit, against the yard heap where night soil and byre litter were composted.
The first is a farm household's own bath; the second is a town's commercial bathhouse open to anyone who pays.
Fruit trees are single trees in the yard near the house; the grove is the farm's stand of windbreak and timber trees.
A trodden earth lane between farmhouses vs a town's streets and drained alleys.
A plank a household lays over a farm ditch, about 4 ft wide, against the road bridges a town builds over its river.
The first is how freight moved and why a landing is the main freight link; the second is the built landing - its piers, quays and stepped banks.
The first is a town's one or two streets and back alleys; the second is a city's planned grid of blocks.
The first is the street a town's lots front; the second is the highway between towns.
A ferry landing is where a road meets an unbridged river; a wharf is where cargo boats load and unload.
An island field is a dry plot raised inside the paddy from its own spoil; the dry fields lie on higher ground beyond the paddy water.
A row village's street is the one line its farms stand along; village lanes join a hamlet's houses to each other and its fields.
How a settlement's name was made from its ground, against how one river carried several names along its course.
The first is the headman's homestead as a whole; the second measures houses, the headman's among them, against an ordinary farmhouse.
A village's landless farm households on a richer farmer's plot, against a town's renters in back-lot tenements.
A half-moon pond is dug before a house or village for fengshui; a reservoir pond holds irrigation water behind a dike above the fields.
The half-moon pond is one fengshui pond before a house or hall; a dike-pond is one of many grow-out fish ponds in the fields.
The ancestral hall is a lineage's own building shared by every household; the butsuma is a room inside one house holding its own dead's tablets.
Pigs and ducks of the paddy village against the chickens and their coop at the farmstead.
A clustered Chinese village's shared woods at chosen places, against the grove each Japanese farmstead keeps round its own house.
The Chinese village's water-mouth grove of many old trees, against the Japanese village's single great tree at its entrance.
The shelter belt topic is the windbreak's sides, trees and lanes; the grove topic is the village's three groves, the back grove serving as its belt.
The coppice is a worked common wood cut for fuel; the fengshui woods are protected groves at the settlement, kept uncut.
The first is how densely any wood was stocked; the second is what the village coppice was and how it was worked.
A charcoal kiln is a single chamber dug into a slope to char wood; a pottery kiln is a climbing chain of firing chambers.
The first is the band of cut grass at a field's edge that kept scrub off; the second is the bund itself.
The first is the grass cut along a channel's bank; the second is how bank, bund and inlet meet where a ditch feeds a field.
The first is the plants of a marsh's margin and the reed cutting; the second is the marsh itself.
The first is the garden's pines and their size; the second is the garden as a whole.
The rack hangs uncut sheaves to dry for weeks, mostly on the paddy; the yard is the floor by the house where they are threshed.
A row village strings its farms in a line, a third form beside the clustered and the scattered village.
